#7575. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7574. Judiciary efforts to create rules for AI stalling amid concerns

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled. (Photo by imaginima/Getty Images)

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled.

The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, which advises the Judicial Conference of the United States, has been developing rules for AI use for several years, but efforts have encountered setbacks and resistance, slowing down the possibility of any new policy.

Attorneys, scholars and judges have criticized proposed evidentiary rules, such as one involving how to handle AI deepfakes, according to a story by Law360.

“Bottom line: I’m not hopeful at this point,” Maura R. Grossman, a professor at the University of Waterloo in Canada whose research has shaped the AI proposals, told Law360.

At the highest levels, there was little immediate reaction from many top European leaders, likely to avoid stoking Trump’s anger.

SÃ¡nchez is one of Europe’s only remaining progressive leaders, and he has repeatedly sparred with Trump over Gaza, the war against Iran, increased military spending and immigration. SÃ¡nchez faces a tough reelection in November with his right-wing foes leading in the polls.

âI feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all â and that’s the cost of living,â Burnham told British broadcasters. âI can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.â

Speaking on French television, Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right National Rally, argued there was no comparison between upcoming French presidential elections and the U.S. midterms. His party’s leader, Marine Le Pen, is leading in polls.

He, too, sought to distinguish National Rally from Trump’s aggressive foreign policy.

âWhat is certain is that in his second term Donald Trump has a clearly different philosophy in his foreign policyâ than in his first term, Bardella said.

In February 2025, Bardella welcomed Trump’s return to the White House, saying his focus on defending national interests represented a âwind of freedom blowing across all Western democracies.â

One of the biggest uncertainties hanging over Europe was what effect the election would have on American policy toward Ukraine.

#7569. Court won’t intervene in California ballot dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

It’s Election Day in the United States. At SCOTUSblog, we’ll be watching not only for race results, but also for new voting-related legal battles. In recent weeks, the Supreme Court has addressed several emergency applications linked to the midterms, and the justices received – and decided – another one on Monday on alleged noncitizen voting in California.

On Monday, the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the justices to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by what it contends are noncitizen voters. Just hours later, the court denied the request. There were no noted dissents. For more on the dispute, see the On Site section below.

Also on Monday, the justices heard argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

On Monday afternoon, the court released its calendar for the January argument session, which will begin on Monday, Jan. 11. Learn about the session in the On Site section.

Today, the justices will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

Tomorrow, the justices will hear argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

WASHINGTON (CN) â The Supreme Court appeared likely Wednesday to shut down a Texas death row inmateâs efforts to use updated medical guidelines to secure another chance at challenging his conviction.

Dexter Johnson didnât initially argue that his execution would violate the Eighth Amendment. But the American Psychiatric Associationâs 2013 edition of its Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, known as DSM-5, adopted new guidelines that classified Johnson as intellectually disabled.

By the time Johnson was convicted of murdering Maria Aparece in 2007, the Supreme Courtâs ruling in Atkins v. Virginia, which held it was unconstitutional to execute a person who is intellectually disabled, had been on the books for five years. But Johnson didnât meet the criteria for such a claim until six years after his conviction.

During his trial, experts testified that Johnson had the intellectual functioning equivalent to a 10-year-old, and his lawyers say he has severe language deficits that place him âwell below the lowest one percentileââ of the population. But his IQ scores of 79 and 88 precluded an intellectual disability diagnosis during his trial and initial appeals.

The DSM-5 moved away from solely focusing on IQ scores, taking into consideration other deficits. And the updated guidelines recognized that individuals with IQ scores over 70 may still qualify as intellectually disabled.

The Anti-Terrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act only permits individuals to file one habeas application unless they can show their claim relies on âa new rule of constitutional law made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court that was previously unavailable.â

The Fifth Circuit found Johnson qualified for the exception, allowing him to proceed with a successive federal habeas application. But on Wednesday, the Supreme Court appeared to disagree.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Donald Trump appointee, questioned if Johnsonâs case would set a precedent for âeternal Atkins claims and zero finalityâ because medical standards around intellectual disability are constantly evolving.

And his conservative colleagues were generally skeptical that claims under the two-decade-old precedent could be considered new.

âDoes Atkins ever stop being a new rule?â Justice Clarence Thomas, a George H.W. Bush appointee, asked.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett, another Trump appointee, compared Johnsonâs definition of new to the invention of the telephone.

âI mean when Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, that was new,â Barrett said. âI don’t think anybody would describe the telephone as new today.â

The liberal wing of the court seemed to side with Johnson, however, stating the Supreme Court in Atkins indicated that who qualifies as intellectually disabled is keyed to medical standards, which can vary and evolve.

As such, Justice Elena Kagan, a Barack Obama appointee, said it was apt to think of Atkins as having multiple rules as those standards have evolved over the last two decades.

âIt would be wrong to think of Atkins as a single rule that we decided exactly when we decided the Atkins case given that Atkins was very cognizant that the substantive standard for the rule was going to be supplied principally by diagnostic criteria,â Kagan said. âSo, if the diagnostic criteria fundamentally changes…you basically get an Atkins II rule, and then the question with respect to that defendant would be whether that is new.â

Instead of considering whether the claims were generally ânew,â Justice Ketani Brown Jackson, a Joe Biden appointee, said the court should consider whether the claim is new to a particular individual.

Despite support from the three Democratic appointees, it did not appear Johnson had enough support from the Republican appointees to reach a majority.

#7567. Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award.

Reuters reported Monday that the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver upheld a $115,000 fee awarded to defense lawyers at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck by the lower court in a trade secrets dispute. The trial court had ruled that the fee was reasonable.

“Plaintiffs have not shown that defense counsel’s use of AI rendered the hours that ​they actually expended unreasonable,” wrote 10th Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh for a unanimous three-judge panel.

The appeals court also upheld the ​dismissal of the lawsuit.

In her opinion, McHugh acknowledged that AI and similar research tools can make attorneys more efficient. But she stressed that lawyers must still verify legal authorities and arguments themselves.

According to Reuters, the case began in 2024, when industrial motor-efficiency equipment maker Flux Drive filed a suit against a Chinese manufacturer, alleging that one of its former engineers had stolen proprietary information and given it to them. After the case was dismissed, Flux Drive was ordered to pay the defendants’ legal fees. On appeal, the company argued that the defense billed for “ministerial tasks,” and that AI use should have lowered the bill.

The defendants countered that their lawyers checked every piece of AI-assisted research, and that Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated entry, redundant task or unreasonable charge.

Brownstein Hyatt partner Christopher Ottele, who represented the defendants, called AI a powerful tool that sophisticated firms should embrace.

“This ​decision confirms that the use of AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still ​must exercise in every filing with the court,” Ottele told Reuters.

Counsel for the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

U.S. District Judge Thomas Thrash Jr. rejected state officialsâ motions to terminate the decree last year, ruling the basic purpose of the agreement had not yet been satisfied and that officials were not meeting outcome measures, including a measure requiring that abuse investigations begin within 24 hours of being reported.

The panel indicated the state is unlikely to receive an answer from the appellate court on whether the agreement should stand. Instead, two judges of the three-judge panel took issue with how Thrash reached his conclusion.

Trump-appointed U.S. Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa agreed, saying, âFor me, this is an easy case. The district court judge applied the incorrect legal standard and they need to go apply the correct legal standard.â

The consent decree came about after a class of children in foster care in two metro Atlanta counties filed a 2002 lawsuit claiming severe neglect and mistreatment. Thompson referenced a raft of “robustâ changes â including the 2022 creation of a sub-agency to fight denials of medically necessary care for foster children â as evidence of âreal, on the ground changeâ the state could point to as evidence of its compliance.

However, Lowrey conceded the case was likely to be remanded back to federal court for new proceedings.

Lagoa and Pryor were joined on the panel by U.S. Circuit Judge Embry Kidd, an appointee of Joe Biden. The panel did not signal when it would issue a decision in the case.

LOS ANGELES (CN) â The man federal prosecutors accuse of starting a brush fire in the early hours of Jan. 1, 2025, that six days later erupted into the devastating Palisades Fire went on trial for a second time Wednesday after a jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict the first time around.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, is charged with two counts of arson. The government argues the Palisades Fire, which destroyed thousands of homes in the affluent Los Angeles neighborhood overlooking the Pacific Ocean, was a so-called holdover from the fire they say Rinderknecht ignited on a hillside near where he had previously lived with a former romantic partner.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew O’Brien told the jury in his opening statement that Rinderknecht was often very angry and was working as an Uber driver that New Year’s Eve. After dropping a passenger in the Palisades shortly before midnight, he parked his car near a trailhead above the houses and hiked up to the “Little Buddha” clearing, where, according to the prosecutor, Rinderknecht had spent a lot of time with his ex.

About 12 minutes after midnight, a nearby surveillance camera captured a fire on the hillside near the clearing while Rinderknecht’s car was still parked below. At the same time, Rinderknecht started calling 911 from a gully a little below the clearing where, O’Brien said, he had ignited the dry brush with a grill lighter.

“It wasn’t an accident,” O’Brien told the jurors. “It was set intentionally.”

It’s not uncommon for an arsonist to call emergency services, he said, because some of them like to watch firefighters battle the blaze they set. Since 911 calls pinpoint the caller’s location even when the call doesn’t go through, investigators knew exactly where Rinderknecht was each time he called.

The location data show Rinderknecht repeatedly dialing 911 while descending the trail back to his car until he had reception again and spoke to an operator. He also started recording himself making the emergency calls, presumably to create an alibi, the prosecutor said.

At the same time, he asked ChatGPT, “Are you at fault if a fire is a lit because of your cigarettes?” The chatbot told him he was.

According to O’Brien, this was an attempt to create an alternative scenario in which he accidentally started the fire.

The fire department had already been alerted by others before Rinderknecht got through to them. He started to drive away from the neighborhood, but when the fire engines passed him going the other way, he turned around, then back to the fire, and remained there for an hour and a half.

The brush fire was quickly put out, but flames continued to smolder underground among the roots of the vegetation, O’Brien told the jury. Six days later, when extreme Santa Ana winds pummeled Southern California, the burning embers underground were stirred back to life, and the Palisades Fire broke out.

Rinderknecht’s attorney, Steven Haney, said in his opening statement that no physical evidence, witnesses or surveillance camera footage connected his client to the start of the Jan. 1 Lachman Fire.

“You’re going to be the gatekeepers of common sense,” he told the jurors.

The attorney argued the prosecution waited until nine months after charging Rinderknecht to test whether the grill lighter they found in Rinderknecht’s car could have set fire to brushes near the Little Buddha clearing. He showed a video of this test in court in which the flames set by the lighter in similar vegetation continued to go out.

“That fire couldn’t get beyond a baking pan,” he said.

As during the first trial last June, Haney told the jury it was more likely that the Jan. 1 fire was caused by New Year’s Eve fireworks, and defense witnesses would testify that they had heard fireworks in the area around midnight. He also said it was disputable his client was the only person in the area at the time.

However, the prosecution pointed to Rinderknecht’s own statements: When investigators interviewed him in the weeks after the fire, he said he was alone at the clearing around midnight, and it was clear and calm.

Also, as during the first trial, Haney argued in his opening statement that Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigators didn’t arrive at the scene and examine the cause of the Jan. 1 fire until after the Palisades Fire had torn through the area and had been left open to hikers and sightseers, thereby obliterating any reliable evidence of how the first fire might have started.

Haney’s animated advocacy almost got Rinderknecht acquitted during the first trial, with only two of the 12 jurors convinced he was guilty.

#7563. The border wall dispute isn’t fit for the emergency docket

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In its latest request to the Supreme Court over President Donald Trump’s approach to immigration, the Justice Department turned to the court’s emergency docket to ask for fast-track permission to construct a border barrier system along a 517-mile stretch in remote west Texas. Stymied by a federal district court’s preliminary injunction issued in October, the Justice Department argues that Supreme Court intervention is needed to prevent irreparable harm to the country. But details of the government’s legal argument reveal that the Trump administration hopes to use the emergency docket as a fast track to victory regardless of the actual urgency of the legal dispute.

Early this year, the Department of Homeland Security began taking important preliminary steps to build physical barriers through Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and nearby property along the U.S.-Mexico border. Part of the Border Patrol’s Big Bend Sector, covering approximately one-quarter of the entire border, no artificial barriers exist there. Despite its massive geographic reach, the region is sparsely populated and at immense distance from large urban centers. Unlike other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, few people or goods cross from one country to the other in the Big Bend Sector. Indeed, according to U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone, who issued a preliminary injunction blocking DHS from carrying out its plans to erect a border barrier in the area, this is the border region with “the lowest aggregate number of apprehensions [of migrants] and the lowest number of apprehensions per mile of border.”

In Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a group of individuals with personal or business ties to the region, along with two advocacy groups, argued that DHS had failed to comply with required environmental reviews. Pointing to a 1996 law signed by President Bill Clinton, the Justice Department responded that Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and his predecessor, Kristi Noem, waived application of those environmental laws. The government also argued that the district court lacked the power to decide the lawsuit in the first place.

Cardone disagreed with the government on both counts. Congress narrowed courts’ jurisdiction in border-barrier disputes, but left room for courts to consider constitutional challenges to DHS’s conduct, she concluded. The challenge to Mullin’s waiver of environmental laws raises a constitutional question, Cardone added.

Having concluded that she could consider the challengers’ lawsuit, Cardone then turned to the criteria that Congress imposed on the secretary of Homeland Security to waive environmental review. The 1996 law directs the immigration agency “to waive all legal requirements” that could slow or impede construction of border barriers and roads. But the same law also instructs DHS to build barriers and roads “in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” Considering the government’s data about apprehensions of people and seizures of drugs in the Big Bend Sector, as compared to other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, Cardone concluded that the region cannot be considered to have high levels of illegal entry. “[I]f the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector,” Cardone announced.

Seven days after Cardone released her opinion, the U.S. solicitor general asked the Supreme Court to intervene. Much of the government’s argument turns on its disagreement with Cardone about what constitutes an area of “high illegal entry.” Mullin determined that the Big Bend Sector constitutes an area of high illegal entry because Customs and Border Protection, the DHS agency that enforces immigration laws at and near the border, apprehended 89,000 people and “seized enormous amounts” of illicit drugs from fiscal years 2021 to 2025, the government explains. In addition, failure to build a border barrier in this region “would act as a dangerous magnet” for additional illegal entries, the solicitor general claims. Despite Mullin’s assessment that the facts on the ground met the “high illegal entry” threshold required by Congress, “the district court nonetheless issued an unprecedented injunction blocking those waivers and halting associated border-wall construction,” the solicitor general wrote to the court.

Unsurprisingly, the challengers disagree. Opposing the government’s request for relief from the justices, they describe Mullin and Noem’s waivers as “unprecedented” and claim they “carry undisputed and extraordinary political and economic significance.”

The solicitor general’s claim is fundamentally a dispute about the proper interpretation of the text of the 1996 law. The government argues that courts cannot second-guess Mullin’s decision to waive environmental laws, and that Mullin’s view of what constitutes “high illegal entry” is all that matters. Cardone disagrees and contends that courts have a role to play here.

By turning to the emergency docket, the Justice Department has dispensed with the ordinary appellate process in favor of a fast-track path to, it hopes, final victory. Wanting an answer sooner rather than later is understandable, but a party’s interest in “line-jumping,” as Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has described the emergency docket, isn’t reason enough to circumvent the slower course of the ordinary appellate process. Jackson would prefer to limit the emergency docket to situations in which an actual emergency exists. It’s hard to see what exigency exists in west Texas, however. The solicitor general argues that drugs and people will continue to enter through the Big Bend Sector. That is undoubtedly true, but, as that stretch of land has been unfortified since it became a border on March 18, 1848, nothing is likely to occur in the near future that is markedly different from past decades.

The government’s request for fast-track intervention by the Supreme Court also does not meet the standards set by Jackson’s ideological opposites. Explaining his view of the court’s emergency docket in Trump v. CASA, the court’s fast-track decision announcing that district courts are not authorized to issue universal injunctions, Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that its alternative pathway is appropriate when “Congress passes a major new statute, or the Executive Branch issues a major new rule or executive order.” Neither applies to the border-wall dispute. Congress enacted the contested statute 30 years ago and the waivers issued by Mullin and Noem are neither an agency rule nor an executive order.

Nor is the border-wall legal battle the type of dispute that only the Supreme Court can resolve. In a 2021 speech, Justice Samuel Alito compared the court’s emergency docket to a hospital’s emergency room, suggesting that, in his view at least, the fast-track process is proper only when no suitable alternative exists. But an alternative does exist to decide if Cardone overstepped. The government could have appealed Cardone’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit. Like other circuit courts, the 5th Circuit regularly reviews preliminary injunctions granted by district courts. As Kavanaugh explained in CASA, “The courts of appeals and this Court can (and regularly do) expeditiously review district court decisions awarding or denying preliminary injunctive relief.”

It is true that Congress has made some challenges to the secretary of Homeland Security’s waiver authority reviewable by the Supreme Court. But it is not clear a dispute over what constitutes an area of high illegal entry fits that requirement. In a 2020 decision, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit explained that the language funneling appeals to the Supreme Court must be interpreted “narrowly.” That court then went on to consider a challenge to border-wall construction in south Texas. And the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, in a case that the D.C. Circuit relied on favorably, distinguished a challenge to the secretary of Homeland Security’s power to waive laws from a challenge to the secretary’s authority to build barriers and roads. The 9th Circuit concluded that it could not review the secretary’s waiver but could review the secretary’s authority to order construction of a border barrier system. A case that “is related to or concerned with the Secretary’s waiver determinations” is not necessarily a challenge to the secretary’s waiver authority, the 9th Circuit explained.

Since Friends of the Ruidosa Church turns on the secretary’s authority to build barriers in areas of high illegal entry, and the government disagrees with Cardone’s interpretation of that section of the 1996 law, the 5th Circuit arguably is empowered to decide whether Cardone is correct. But instead of asking the 5th Circuit to correct the mistake it claims Cardone committed, the solicitor general skipped the 5th Circuit and went directly to the Supreme Court.

The reason it did this is not difficult to figure out: The administration is hopeful that it will receive a friendly audience at the Supreme Court. But this is a fast-track procedure meant for exceptional circumstances. And there is nothing exceptional about the legal fight over the administration’s attempt to build new segments of border barrier in rural west Texas. If the court grants the government’s request to pause Cardone’s preliminary injunction, allowing construction to move forward where no barrier currently exists, it should, at the very least, explain how this case meets the criteria that the justices have previously provided and if the term “emergency docket” is a misnomer.

A prior version of this article did not include the paragraphs beginning with “It is true that” and “Since Friends of the Ruidosa Church.”

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

#7562. Rhode Island Hospital asks Fifth Circuit to axe DOJ subpoena for trans patient records

The hospital argues the subpoena was issued for the improper purpose of pressuring it to end gender-affirming care.

(CN) â Rhode Island Hospital asked the Fifth Circuit Wednesday to reverse a federal judge’s order requiring it to comply with a Justice Department subpoena seeking extensive information on the hospital’s treatment of transgender youth, including patient records.

The hospital’s attorney, Matthew Fitzgerald, told a three-judge panel that the order â which was entered the same day the government filed its petition â was issued without due process, as the hospital wasn’t given a chance to respond. He also argued the Justice Department lacked a legitimate purpose for investigating the hospital’s provision of gender-affirming care, saying its real goal was to use a burdensome subpoena to pressure the hospital into stopping such treatment since the feds reached settlements with at least six other hospitals requiring them to do just that.

“Imagine a future Department of Justice that is against the AR-15 rifle,” Fitzgerald said. “So they say, ‘We’re going to investigate the manufacturers of this rifle on suspicion of something â aiding and abetting, perhaps, the drug cartels in Mexico. We’re going to send them subpoenas. We’re going to ask for the personnel files of everyone at the company, everyone involved in the manufacture of these guns, the entire files. We’re going to ask for any contact information they have for the buyer of every AR-15 rifle for the last six years.’ And when the gun companies squeal and say it’s unduly burdensome, it’s for an improper purpose, the government says, ‘Well, if you stop manufacturing this rifle, we’ll claim victory and go away.’”

Justice Department attorney John Bailey said the government is lawfully investigating potential violations of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. While it is legal for doctors in Rhode Island to prescribe puberty-blocking drugs and cross-sex hormones for the treatment of gender dysphoria â a use for which they have not been approved by the FDA â it is not legal for drug manufacturers and distributors to promote such off-label use. Bailey insisted the Justice Department is seeking evidence from Rhode Island Hospital showing such improper promotion by manufacturers and distributors.

But U.S. Circuit Judge Irma Ramirez questioned why the government is seeking patient records if it’s targeting drugmakers.

“If you are investigating whether the manufacturers are misbranding the drugs, then why not start with the manufacturers or limit the scope of the subpoena to communications to the hospital or to the doctors about these allegedly misbranded drugs?” the Joe Biden appointee asked. “Why ask for patient files and personnel files?”

Although the hospital is in Rhode Island, the government filed its petition for enforcement in the Fort Worth division of the Northern District of Texas, where the two active federal judges are both deeply conservative.

Bailey told the Fifth Circuit panel that the hospital is producing responsive records, with patient information anonymized, for the Texas federal court to hold privately while the two appeals are resolved.

U.S. Circuit Judges Kyle Duncan and Kurt Engelhardt, both Trump appointees, criticized the hospital for filing a motion to quash in another court after O’Connor ruled. Duncan said the hospital had created a “procedural conundrum” through parallel proceedings, and Engelhardt called its actions a “sharp practice” that potentially raises ethical concerns.

But Fitzgerald said the case in Rhode Island was started by the Child Advocate, and he argued the hospital was justified in joining that challenge to the subpoena because O’Connor’s order was void for lack of due process.

In July 2025, the Trump administration announced it had issued “more than 20 subpoenas” to doctors and clinics that provide gender-affirming care to minors. This followed an executive order from Trump calling for an end to such treatments, which the president described as âthe maiming and sterilizing of a growing number of impressionable young children.â

Numerous federal judges have blocked or limited these subpoenas, but in August a divided three-judge panel of the Ninth Circuit â the only federal appeals court to have ruled on the issue thus far â overturned a federal judge’s order quashing such a subpoena. A George W. Bush appointee and a Donald Trump appointee ruled, over the dissent of a Bill Clinton appointee, that the lower court was wrong in finding the subpoena was issued for an improper purpose. The clinic targeted by that subpoena has sought rehearing by the full appeals court.

#7561. Trial opens for suspect whose multiple email threats include ‘skinning’ federal judge

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.” (Image from Shutterstock)

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.”

David Brooks Pokorny, 45, of El Cerrito, California, allegedly sent 11 email threats in a span of 44 minutes to assault, kidnap and murder Breyer, a senior judge for the Northern District of California, according to U.S. Assistant Attorney Kent Stejskal in opening statements Tuesday.

“Words within those 11 emails constitute what are called true threats,” said Stejskal, according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

He allowed the 14-person jury to view snippets of the emails during the trial. Pokorny is charged with making felony threats against a judicial officer and faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

According to Pokorny’s public defender John Reichmuth, his client’s words were “truly shocking, truly offensive, truly ugly, but not true threats.”

Reichmuth said the emails were free speech, and the prosecution would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Pokorny, who has a history of sending threats to public officials and media outlets, meant to perform the actions described in his emails.

Presiding U.S. District Judge Jon Tigar of the Northern District of California noted that the prosecution does not have to prove that Pokorny intended to carry out the threat for it to supersede the protections of First Amendment free speech rights.

#7560. Ex-prisoner argues liability of US companies over slave labor abroad

The Seventh Circuit asked if the Trafficking Victims Protection Act gave American courts jurisdiction over accusations of forced labor in American manufacturing facilities abroad.

CHICAGO (CN) â A former political prisoner of a Chinese prison maintained Wednesday before a Seventh Circuit panel that a Wisconsin-based company should be held responsible for violations of federal forced labor laws.

The plaintiff accused Milwaukee Tool Corporation in 2024 of cramping him and other prisoners in a grueling manufacturing facility and exploiting them for the production of Milwaukee Tool’s gloves.

The plaintiff’s attorney Jennifer Bennett argued before the three-judge panel that an amendment of the Trafficking Victims Protection Act â a 2000 law enacted to eliminate modern forms of slavery â grants U.S. courts extra-territorial jurisdiction over any offense, civil or criminal.

“That’s for two reasons, each of which is independently sufficient to reverse. First, this lawsuit is a domestic application of the statute,” Bennett, an attorney with San Francisco-based firm Gupta Wessler LLP, said. “Second, even if an American company profiting in the U.S. from its U.S. participation is not a domestic application, the statute applies extraterritorially, whether it is criminally or civilly enforced.”

The plaintiff brought his claims under subsection 1589(b) of the act, which prohibits âknowingly benefit[ing] … from participation in a venture which has engagedâ in forced labor. But a lower court determined that although the statute grants the government extra-territorial jurisdiction, it does not apply when the statute is enforced civilly.

Chief U.S. Circuit Judge Michael Brennan pressed Bennett further on her understanding of the statute.

“Would your reading make the civil remedy reach farther with fewer safeguards than the criminal prosecution that it rests on?” the Donald Trump appointee asked.

“I don’t think so, your honor, because the civil provision directly only applies to the predicates prohibited by the statute, and so the extraterritorial reach of the civil provision would not be greater than any of the predicates that the remedies enforce,” Bennett said.

Milwaukee Tool’s attorney David Horniak maintained that Bennett wrongfully interpreted the extraterritoriality provision of the act to apply not only to criminal prosecutions, but also to civil remedies.

“We are not looking for whether one can squint at the statute and find a way to read it to apply to civil actions,” Horniak, an attorney at Washington-based firm DLA Piper LLP, said. “We are looking for whether Congress gave us clear, unmistakable instruction.”

U.S. Circuit Judge Joshua Kolar raised concerns about comity, given that the Fourth Circuit ruled in favor of the plaintiff in a 2019 case, in which the plaintiff sought relief after she was sexually abused while working as a housekeeper in the U.S. Embassy in Yemen.

“We’re a little bit worried about just letting anyone dabble in international relations, right? So, if you don’t have that rule, how do you account for that?” the Barack Obama appointee asked.

Bennett noted that the extraterritorially provision is not limited to U.S. citizens, it also applies to companies and people that are present in the United States.

“I think this statute makes it very clear that Congress was thinking about international trafficking, the entire statute is about international trafficking. Congress expanded the extraterritorial jurisdiction at the same time,” Bennett said. “It expanded the cause of action to ensure that it applied to every offense under the TVPA, the findings in the statute explicitly say the reason the United States is getting involved in this is because we don’t think foreign countries are doing it good enough job.â©In other words, Congress itself is making that balance.”

Horniak rebuffed Bennett’s characterization of the statute.

“I think this case raises a paradigm example of the kinds of comity concerns that could have motivated Congress not to extend [the statute] extraterritorially,” Horniak said. “While Milwaukee Tool is the defendant, the underlying conduct at issue here is alleged forced labor in Chinese prisons by the Chinese government.”

“Imagine France enacted a similar law enabling former prisoners in the United States to sue in France for alleged violations of French law based on how they were treated in U.S. prisons,” he added.

Alongside Judges Brennan and Kolar, U.S. Circuit Judge Kenneth Ripple, a Ronald Reagan appointee, also sat on the panel Wednesday. The judges did not indicate when they might rule on the matter.

#7559. Ignition, Inc.: MSP Mac Help Desk Guru (work from home)

Ignition is one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and the only fractional IT firm that specializes in the venture-backed technology ecosystem.

Fully Remote · Work from home · Full-time (Eastern or Pacific time zones) · Apple-first

ignitionit.com is a seasoned, Apple-first MSP — in business for almost 30 years — and we're hiring a Help Desk Technician to be the friendly, capable first voice our clients reach when something isn't working. This position is a remote, work-from-home, full-time role.

We've written this as a junior-to-mid-level job description because that's where most great people start on our team. But if you're more seasoned — comfortable in identity, MDM, or security work — don't scroll past. We'd be delighted to find someone who can step in higher up the ladder, and we'll happily talk about a more senior scope and comp if that's you.

Unlike many IT shops, we believe that the technology is the tactic. The actual job is making people feel taken care of. One of our core values is “49% tech support, 51% human support.”

You'll succeed by configuring devices, resetting access, untangling email, and chasing down the gremlin that's been haunting someone's conference room. But you'll know you succeeded when a client exhales and says, “Thank goodness you're on it!” That Warm Fuzzy Feeling™ is the actual product. The green lights on the dashboard are just how we get there.

Onboard a new hire at a fast-growing startup: provision their Mac, set up their Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 accounts, enroll the device in MDM, and make sure day one feels effortless.

Offboard a departing employee cleanly — recover the laptop, revoke access, and close the loop so nothing's left dangling. All boxes checked, ticket notated and closed, client followed up with.

Field a "my email stopped working" ticket that turns out to be a DNS thing, a phishing-filter thing, or a "they changed their password on their phone three weeks ago" thing.

Help a family office or RIA get a touchy Zoom Room or conference-room AV setup behaving before a meeting — over the phone.

Triage the queue so phones get answered fast, emails don't rot, and nobody feels forgotten — even when the honest answer is, “We're on it, but here's the realistic timeline."

⠀ You'll be the front line: helping with what you can, researching what you can't, and pinging the rest of the team when you're genuinely stuck. That last part is a skill, not a weakness — knowing when to ask is half the job.

We're one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and one of the only certified Apple Premier Partners — that’s kinda like getting knighted by the ghost of Steve Jobs. We started where you’d expect to find Macs (creative agencies, non-profits, education) but our primary clients today are cutting-edge, venture-backed AI SaaS startups, VC and private equity firms, registered investment advisors — many of them operating under stringent compliance expectations (SOC 2, SEC). That means we hold ourselves to a higher standard than the scrappy shop we started as. Polished, reliable, security-minded work is the baseline now — but always with a smile!

What hasn't changed: relationships are still our most valuable currency — with clients, with vendors, and with each other. We're a tight, supportive team. We teach each other what we know, cover for each other when life throws a punch, and care a little too much about doing things the right way. We're still a bit weird, and our clients seem to like us that way.

We move fast, priorities shift, it’s not always documented (whatever it is), our tool set and list of supported platforms is sprawling, and some days the to-do list is longer than you'd like. If you can stay warm under pressure, create order out of chaos, learn new stuff fast because you love it, and speak up when you need help, you'll thrive here.

If you need a rigid, fully-documented, never-changes environment where nobody trusts you with admin access, where you will be micro-managed so you never have to wonder whether or not you’re doing the right thing, this isn't it. You’ll have a ton of independence on our team, and freedom to use your best judgment to get the ball over the finish line, but that also means we expect you to be naturally responsible, honest, and highly accountable — to yourself, your teammates, and the clients. As they say, the price of freedom is eternal vigilance.

The tech you'll work with (and grow into)

Apple at the core — macOS, iOS, Apple Business Manager, and MDM (Jamf / Iru / Intune / Workspace ONE / and more)

Yes, PCs too — about one-third of our users are driving Windows

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 admin consoles

Identity and access — SSO, MFA, and security keys (Okta, Entra ID, Yubikey, and friends)

Lots of other security tools — our stack is constantly evolving and may vary from client to client

The everyday productivity stack — Slack, Zoom, conference-room AV, networking basics (Meraki), and endpoint tooling

⠀ You don't need to know all of this. You need to be the kind of person who wants to. As you grow, there's a clear path into infrastructure administration, project architecture and implementation, and — for the right person — security and compliance work (phishing simulations, endpoint detection, SOC 2 / CIS / SEC readiness, due diligence questionnaire support, etc.). That's where our most senior people live, and it's wide open.

The hard requirements — we won't move forward unless you:

Can work standard business hours in Eastern or Pacific time zones (we currently need both)

Have a quiet home workspace and reliable broadband

Have proven Apple aptitude — you actually use and like the Apple ecosystem

Have at least 5 years of IT support experience on the job.

⠀ Everything else — and this is the longer list, on purpose. We figure technical skills are teachable; character takes a lot longer. So we're looking for someone who:

Genuinely cares — about clients, teammates, and doing right by people

Loves to learn, and proves it in how they spend their time

Reads, and writes clearly — clear writing is clear thinking, and you'll do a lot of it

Stays calm and kind with a frustrated person on the other end of the line

Can tell the difference between good customer service and fantastic customer service, and refuses to settle for the former

Notices when something's being done inefficiently and fixes it (you may boast about it later, that’s fine)

Proofreads their own work (yes, we noticed whether you proofread your application)

Has a sense of humor, and doesn't take themselves too seriously

Our company founder/CEO is headquartered in the Bay Area. We work with innovative, ambitious companies developing AI products. Our team members hold a range of opinions about whether AI is “good or bad” for humans, but at the end of the day, we embrace the plain fact that it is here, we must embrace it to evolve, and our clients increasingly depend on us to help them embrace it, too, to help them evolve and stay competitive.

Our CEO's opinion: AI will not replace human labor any time soon; rather, AI is a new opportunity to either (a) get things done faster, or (b) get a much higher quality of output than before. If you’re an AI tinkerer, great! We want to hear how you’re using it and see your latest vibe project. If you’re allergic to AI or have no interest in learning new habits to work effectively with it, this is not the place for you.

Base salary: Applicants outside the USA will be compensated according to your local employment market. For applicants closer to the junior side who are located in the USA, $50,000–$65,000/yr, depending on experience level and your local geographical price index. With experience, comp goes up from there. Genuinely experienced, more senior candidates can be slotted higher — let's talk.

Type & location: Full-time, work from home, fully remote. Eastern or Pacific time zones.

Benefits: Medical / dental / vision for the employee, 401(k) with employer contribution, 2 weeks of PTO annually to start, and a stipend for your home internet.

Take this online Culture Index assessment (about 10 minutes): We use it to screen for people whose natural wiring fits how our team works.

If your profile lines up with what we're looking for, we'll reach out and ask you to complete a 60-minute TestGorilla assessment for critical thinking skills, send us your resume, and maybe a couple of other items.

From there, we conduct between 2-4 video interviews. One of these might be a live technical assessment.

If the Culture Index step feels like a strange way to start a job application — that's kind of the point. Remember the phrase Think Different?

Ignition is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome and will consider all qualified applicants. Good luck in your search — and may the Force be with you!

Remember every detail and next step, without a meeting bot.

#7558. Will an ability to hold federal officers accountable survive this term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

At a time when there is a desire to hold ICE agents accountable for their constitutional violations, the Supreme Court might be poised to eliminate the only way to hold them civilly liable under federal law.

By way of background, if state or local officers violate the Constitution, they can be sued under a federal statute, 42 U.S.C. Section 1983. But no federal law authorizes suits against federal officers for constitutional violations. Rather, the ability to sue a federal government officer for money damages comes from a 1971 Supreme Court decision, Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. There, the court said that it would allow a cause of action for money damages under the Fourth Amendment even without a federal statute authorizing it.

Nevertheless, for decades, the Supreme Court has refused to extend or even apply Bivens to other violations of constitutional rights by federal officers, and several conservative justices have called for it to be overruled. Now, in Nielsen v. Watanabe, to be argued on Nov. 9, the court will again confront whether to allow a Bivens suit – and perhaps whether to end such claims entirely.

The underlying issue is about separation of powers: should the court provide a remedy for constitutional violations or is that entirely the province of Congress? But it also is about accountability: without Bivens, how can those who violate constitutional rights, including ICE agents, be held responsible and how can those injured be compensated?

Webster Bivens alleged that he had been subjected to an illegal and humiliating search by agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. Bivens sought money damages as compensation for the harms he suffered. The court held that a federal law cause of action for money damages could be inferred directly from the Fourth Amendment. The majority, in an opinion by Justice William Brennan, emphasized that individuals whose rights have been violated should not be relegated to state law remedies, which might be inadequate or hostile to the federal constitutional interest.

In an important and often-cited concurring opinion, Justice John Marshall Harlan explained that the federal courts long have devised remedies for violations of federal law. Harlan said that it is essential that federal courts be able to provide such relief because “it is apparent that some form of damages is the only possible remedy for someone in Bivens’ alleged position. … For people in Bivens’ shoes, it is damages or nothing.” Harlan rejected the claim that the court violates separation of powers when it creates such a cause of action and remedy. In his view, the court is responsible for upholding and enforcing the Bill of Rights, and, hence, the judiciary need not wait for the legislature in order to act.

Chief Justice Warren Burger and Justices Hugo Black and Harry Blackmun dissented. Each wrote an opinion arguing that separation of powers means that Congress, and not the court, should create a cause of action for damages against federal officers. Black explained that “[s]hould the time come when Congress desires such lawsuits, it has before it a model of valid legislation, 42 U.S.C. §1983, to create a damage remedy against federal officers.” Similarly, Blackmun argued that “it is the Congress, and not this Court, that should act.”

For a decade after Bivens, the court applied and extended it. In 1979’s Davis v. Passman, the court allowed a Bivens suit under the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment for an equal protection claim. Congressman Otto Passman fired his administrative assistant, Shirley Davis, because he wanted a male to fill the position. In allowing the suit against the congressman, the court emphasized the judiciary's role in ensuring effective protection of constitutional rights.

And only a year later, in Carlson v. Green, the court allowed a Bivens suit for violation of the Eighth Amendment. A mother sued federal prison officials on behalf of her deceased son, claiming that he was the victim of gross inadequacies of medical facilities and staff, which caused his death and constituted cruel and unusual punishment. A remedy was available under the Federal Tort Claims Act; thus, the issue before the court was whether a Bivens suit should be allowed in light of this alternative. The court concluded that Bivens suits were a “counterpart” to the Federal Tort Claims Act because the act creates liability for the federal government and a Bivens cause of action permits recovery from federal officers themselves. The court found no indication that Congress intended for the act to preclude Bivens suits.

Since 1980, however, the court has not ruled in favor of a Bivens claim. In its most recent decision about Bivens, 2022’s Egbert v. Boule, the court noted that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.”

Specifically, the court has held that that such claims are not allowed if there is a statute that precludes suits (in 2010’s Hui v. Castaneda), or that provides an alternative remedy even if it is inadequate (in 1988’s Schweiker v. Chilicky). It has precluded Bivens claims for those injured while in the military, even for egregious violations of their rights (in 1987’s United States v. Stanley). It has ruled that Bivens suits should be allowed only if they are on balance desirable and consistently has found that they are not (in 2007’s Wilkie v. Robbins, 2017’s Ziglar v. Abbasi, 2020’s Hernandez v. Mesa, and Boule). And it has precluded Bivens suits against private prisons that contract with the federal government (in 2001’s Correctional Services Corp. v. Malesko) and the guards employed by them (in 2012’s Minecci v. Pollard).

Based on this line of cases, the court in Egbert v. Boule stressed that recognizing a Bivens cause of action “is ‘a disfavored judicial activity.’” The court stated that

The court then laid out the framework for Bivens claims going forward. According to the majority, this should be guided by a two-step inquiry:

This is a test that puts a very strong presumption against recognizing Bivens claims.

Like Carlson v. Green, Nielsen v. Watanabe involves an Eighth Amendment claim for cruel and unusual punishment.The case involves a prisoner, Kekai Watanabe, who alleges that he suffered a broken tailbone when attacked by other prisoners that caused him excruciating pain and that a staff nurse, Francis Nielsen, denied him medical care. The court granted review as to whether the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit “erred [here] in recognizing a Bivens cause of action.”

Watanabe argues to the court that this case is governed by Carlson v. Green and does not seek to extend Bivens in any way. His brief states: “Watanabe asserts the same kind of violation of the same constitutional right by the same type of defendant in the same institutional setting pursuant to the same substantive standards as the plaintiff in Carlson. This is precisely the kind of claim this Court has long understood Carlson to encompass.”

In response, Nielsen argues that Bivens suits are strongly disfavored and that there are “significant factual differences such as the immediacy and severity of the harm alleged” compared with Carlson. But that is not all: Nielsen also expressly argues that “Bivens should be overruled” and that “Congress, not the judiciary, creates causes of action.”

The court could affirm the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit and allow a Bivens suit, saying that this is governed by Carlson. Or the court could distinguish Carlson, accepting Nielsen’s argument that there are sufficient factual differences between the cases, essentially limiting Bivens claims only for cruel and unusual punishment claims involving deaths. Or the court could overrule Carlson but not overrule Bivens.

Or the court could overrule Bivens entirely, which several conservative justices have advocated in the past.

The fundamental disagreement, as it was in Bivens, is whether it is the judicial role to provide remedies for violations of constitutional rights or whether that is just for Congress. The practical reality is that without Bivens suits, those whose rights have been violated – even horribly – are left with no recourse. In Hernandez v. Mesa, for example, a boy in Mexico was killed by shot fired across the border by a federal agent in Texas. The court’s rejection of a Bivens suit left no remedy at all.

In that case, and in many other situations, the Federal Tort Claims Act does not allow suits against the United States. Often there are not state tort remedies available either. To paraphrase Justice Harlan, for people in the shoes of many injured by federal officers, it is Bivens suits or nothing.

I would like to think that the reports of egregious constitutional violations by ICE agents, including killings, would cause the court to realize the importance of Bivens suits and to not end such causes of action. That is what makes Nielsen v. Watanabe so important.

Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

“We always seek the best possible relationship with the United States â one that ensures respect for our sovereignty and territorial integrity, and is based on collaboration without subordination,” she said.

When mentioning trade relations with the U.S., Sheinbaum noted talks under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement go through the executive branch and not Congress.

The U.S. declined to renew the USMCA trade agreement in July and review of the agreement, which is in effect until 2036, will continue on a yearly basis or until all three countries agree to sign an extension.

Tony Payan, the executive director of the Claudio X. GonzÃ¡lez Center for the U.S. and Mexico at Rice Universityâs Baker Institute for Public Policy said that a lot of what Trump does with Mexico depends a lot on how the Democrats handle him.

“There are some things that I think Trump understands well, and I think he probably understands that he got a beating and that he is largely responsible for it,” said Payan. “He told people to ‘make as if I were on the ballot.’ And the people gave him a flunking no.”

#7556. Court seems poised to side with Catholic preschools in religious discrimination dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared ready to hold that the exclusion of Catholic preschools in Colorado from the state’s universal preschool program violates the First Amendment. After just over two hours of oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a majority seemed to agree with the challengers that Colorado’s refusal to provide them with an exemption from rules that would require the preschools to admit all students – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents – should be subject to a more stringent constitutional test than that applied by the lower court. The court could decide to apply that standard itself or send the case back to the lower courts for them to do so.

Colorado launched the universal preschool program, which provides families in the state with up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools, in 2023. To participate in the program, preschools must meet a variety of state standards and sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” The preschools cannot decline to serve LGBTQ families, because Colorado believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.

The plaintiffs – the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children – went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy. They contended that requiring Catholic preschools to agree to the nondiscrimination agreement to participate in the universal preschool program constitutes unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to carve out a religious exemption that allows them to take part in the program.

After both the district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected the challengers’ claim, they came to the Supreme Court last year, asking the justices to take up the case – which the court agreed in April 2026 to do.

Representing the challengers, Nicholas Reaves told the justices that the schools in the Archdiocese of Denver “exist to pass on the faith to the next generation.” “[T]his is not a zero-sum game,” he said, because “letting Catholic schools” participate in the universal preschool program “will create more seats for everyone.”

Representing the state, Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton countered that “Colorado welcomes religious preschools to” the program and allows them to teach their religious beliefs. It simply asks them, she emphasized, to comply with the same rules as everyone else.

One of the major points of contention at Tuesday’s argument was the significance of the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction. The case was the third in a trilogy of decisions on the availability of public funding for religious institutions. In Carson, the majority applied strict scrutiny – the toughest constitutional test – after it concluded that the Maine law barred some private schools from receiving public funds “solely because they are religious.”

In response to a question from Justice Clarence Thomas about whether a ruling for the challengers would require the court to extend its ruling in Carson, Reaves responded that it would not. In Carson, he insisted, the court’s “focus … was to look at … what is happening to the religious believer?” The court in Carson, he said, “didn’t focus on the text of the law in Maine. It focused on whether schools are being excluded on account of their religious exercise.”

Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Reaves on that point, observing that the law at issue in Carson specifically discriminated against religious schools – which, Roberts suggested, is not the case with the Colorado program.

Reaves pushed back. He noted that the laws in other cases involving public benefits had been neutral, rather than discriminating against religious people or organizations – for example, the court’s 1963 decision in Sherbert v. Verner, reversing a ruling by the South Carolina Supreme Court that had rejected a constitutional challenge to the denial of employment benefits from a Seventh-day Adventist whose religion barred her from working on Saturday.

Roberts later questioned Norton on a related point, asking her to differentiate the Colorado program from the law at issue in Carson and telling her that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here.” He also told Norton that the state was trying to “bury Sherbert” even though “nothing in our precedent has backed away from” it.

Two of the court’s Democratic appointees, however, echoed Roberts’ initial skepticism that Carson dictated the outcome of the challengers’ case. Justice Elena Kagan told Reaves that the trilogy of cases culminating in Carson involved laws that had excluded religious institutions and schools because of their religion. “[I]t was a nondiscrimination principle,” she emphasized, but “you’re asking us to” issue a decision that would go “far beyond” its earlier cases. In particular, she suggested, the challengers were seeking a ruling that religious people “need a special accommodation” because of their faith.

Reaves responded that an interpretation of the court’s decision in Carson that focused on whether the law at issue expressly discriminated against religion would be “very easy to circumvent.”

Kagan responded that this isn’t “a good case to raise the kind of specter of circumvention.” “[T]his is a case,” she continued, “of a state trying to enforce its own nondiscrimination principles.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to agree. She characterized Carson as a case that prohibited governments from treating religious schools worse than it treated secular schools. That doctrine, she posited, was “pretty narrow” and made “perfect sense.” But, she told Reaves, “your schools want to discriminate by exclusion” when no other school participating in the universal preschool program does so.

Some of the court’s Republican appointees were more persuaded by the challengers’ argument – also advanced by Sarah Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general who argued on behalf of the Trump administration in support of the challengers – that Carson should apply even if the Colorado law does not specifically target religion.

Justice Neil Gorsuch, for example, asked “what would be left” of cases like Sherbert “if everything turned on express discrimination” against religion, while Justice Samuel Alito appeared dubious that the legislators who enacted the Colorado universal preschool law “would not understand what the effect of” the law’s requirements “would be.”

Similarly, Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Norton why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows “schools will be unable to agree to?” Barrett pointed to a New York Times op-ed written in the wake of Carson by law professor Aaron Tang, who she stated suggested that states counteract some of the effects of Carson by enacting nondiscrimination requirements.

Norton resisted any effort to link Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement to an intent to target religious schools, stressing that there was no evidence of the legislature’s motives and (in response to a question from Jackson) that the requirement predated the inclusion of religious schools in the program.

The justices and advocates also debated, although less extensively than the significance of Carson, whether Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that are subject to a less stringent constitutional test, known as rational-basis review.

Reaves told the justices that the Colorado nondiscrimination requirement was not the kind of “across-the-board” prohibition that the court envisioned in Smith because the Colorado law contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catch-all” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation. Moreover, he added, the law also creates exceptions to accommodate children with disabilities and children from low-income families.

For her part, Norton characterized the preferences as very different from the kind of exclusion that the challengers seek. Even if a school receives a preference, she stressed, it is still subject to the nondiscrimination requirement.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh appeared to approach the case from what he regarded as a practical angle, asking Norton why the state wouldn’t “seek the win/win?” With over 2,000 preschools participating in the Colorado program, he said, there should be “plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers” and, at the same time, “the ability of LGBT parents” to find a school that is a good fit for their families. “Why,” he asked, “has this been provoked?”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor took a different tack, suggesting that a ruling for the challengers could have broader implications. A Catholic preschool, she told Reaves, could reject a child “merely” because his or her parents are LGBTQ. Would this, she queried, also allow a religious preschool to turn down Black children?

Reaves said that it would not. He pointed to a 1983 case in which the Supreme Court, applying strict scrutiny, upheld the Internal Revenue Service’s decision to revoke the tax-exempt status of a private university and private school with racially discriminatory admissions policies. The government in that case, he emphasized, indicated that its interest in prohibiting such policies was not merely “compelling” (the first factor under strict scrutiny) but “overriding.”

He told the justices that strict scrutiny should similarly apply to this case. “And then the government can come forward and say we have a really good reason for” excluding Catholic preschools from the program. But, he concluded, “we just don’t think they’ve done that in this case.”

By the end of the argument, Sotomayor seemed to leave little doubt about where she stood. “No matter what line of cases we follow,” she said, “there will be tremendous problems and a great cost to someone.”

A decision is expected sometime next year.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7555. BigLaw partners with Big Tech to design and deploy custom AI tools

In recent months, Big Tech has invested heavily in law.

On Oct. 15, Microsoft unveiled Copilot for legal, which builds on what it previously introduced as its Legal Agent in Word. In September, OpenAI debuted Astra for Law: GPT-6 Astra, a new model that is tailored for professional legal work. One month earlier, Google announced Gemini Enterprise for Legal. And in May, Anthropic introduced Claude for Legal.

At the same time, several BigLaw firms have increased their investment in generative artificial intelligence. Rather than just using these platforms, they are working with major tech providers to build their own custom AI tools. As part of these partnerships, they receive the resources needed to design specific solutions that fit their workflows, while OpenAI and others see firsthand how AI is shaping the legal practice.

Sullivan & Cromwell was one firm that teamed up with OpenAI to develop a new tool and announced its collaboration at the same time as the Astra for Law model. Called the Agreement Analyzer, it integrates the firm’s workflows with OpenAI’s ChatGPT Enterprise and analyzes agreements using select precedents and negotiating playbooks from the firm or its clients.

The tool provides a more thorough analysis of those materials than any standard large language model and not only identifies potential issues, but includes rationales for them and ways to address them, says John Savva, a partner at Sullivan & Cromwell who created the Agreement Analyzer and worked with OpenAI to refine it.

Sullivan & Cromwell’s lawyers already used ChatGPT, so teaming up with OpenAI seemed like a logical next step, Savva says.

“They were looking for law firms to collaborate with to see what law firms and OpenAI working together could develop and what potential that would hold for the future,” Savva says. “Since we already had prototypes in hand, it was natural for us to see what we could do to further develop those with OpenAI.”

Initially, the Agreement Analyzer could be used by one individual at a time, but OpenAI engineers helped Savva modify it so that it could be more broadly available in just a few months, he says. An initial trial group is testing and providing feedback on the tool, which will eventually be rolled out to the entire firm.

“It’s really shown us that you can take a tool very rapidly from a draft prototype to something that could be deployed through a collaboration like this,” Savva says.

Ropes & Gray was another early partner of OpenAI. Ahead of Astra for Law’s launch, the firm worked with OpenAI to develop an AI-powered tool that speeds up the diligence review process.

The tool replicates the exact steps the firm’s attorneys take when they dig into large volumes of documents, including identifying risks and critical issues, and it produces a comprehensive diligence report in just hours. With those reports quickly in hand, attorneys can spend more time providing strategic counsel to clients before transactions.

Currently in the testing phase, the tool is consistently providing better results than other off-the-shelf diligence applications, says Josh Lichtenstein, a partner at Ropes & Gray who helps deploy AI at the firm.

“What the process looked like for us was a combination of the engineering expertise from OpenAI plus our own vision as lawyers of how a tool should work,” says Lichtenstein, who noted Ropes & Gray began working with the tech provider about three months ago. “And it was really the combination of the two that led to, I think, a much better outcome than we would have gotten otherwise.”

In addition to OpenAI, Ropes & Gray speaks regularly with Anthropic, Google and other tech providers about new AI tools and how to incorporate AI in their work, says Howard Glazer, a partner and head of practice AI at the firm.

“We will talk to anyone,” Glazer says. “As a firm, we are total believers that AI will transform the industry, and so we are intent on being at the front of the wave.”

These partnerships are mutually advantageous, he adds. While tech providers learn more about the inner workings of the legal profession, Ropes & Gray is creating cutting-edge solutions that ultimately benefit its clients.

As another example, the firm partnered with AI-powered contract drafting company Draftwise to deploy its legal ontology platform within its private funds practice. It connects and structures partnership agreements, side letters and other insights from the firm’s fund formation work and allows lawyers to access and leverage the collective experience to enhance negotiations.

“Where it adds the most value for clients, we forge partnerships to build capabilities around our own methods and experience,” Glazer says. “Our partnerships with OpenAI and Draftwise tie back to our broader AI strategy—building AI around our clients’ needs and our relationships with them, and using that knowledge to amplify our lawyers’ judgment.”

Among other firms partnering with Big Tech is Freshfields. The London-based firm announced in April that it would collaborate with Anthropic to deliver AI-native legal services as well as create novel AI legal workflows.

“Our approach in the Freshfields Lab has always been to build on the best available technology. Claude’s capabilities have become an essential part of our proprietary AI-powered solutions,” said Gerrit Beckhaus, partner and co-head of Freshfields Lab, in a statement. “With this collaboration, we are going further: co-developing agentic workflows with Anthropic that can handle multistep legal tasks end-to-end. For our clients, that translates into faster, more precise and more scalable legal services.”

There is plenty of room for bespoke AI tools in the legal profession, says Savva, who expects to see more as the delivery of legal services continues to evolve.

“Firms will, I think, frequently want to develop a tool that differentiates their approach from those of others,” Savva says. “Just as lawyers and firms have differentiated approaches, the tools will naturally have differentiated approaches as well.”
